title: Kenyan Coconut Cake
author: Chef Amina Hassan
desc: Kenyan Coconut Cake — a moist, tender cake made with coconut milk, desiccated coconut, and cardamom, baked until golden and fragrant. The definitive Kenyan celebration cake — served at birthdays, Eid, weddings, and every occasion that calls for something truly special. The 150th and final Kenyan recipe on GieesK Recipes.
longDesc: Kenyan Coconut Cake is the celebration cake of the Swahili coast — baked for Eid feasts, birthday gatherings, wedding receptions, and homecoming celebrations across coastal Kenya and beyond. The coconut milk in the batter keeps the crumb extraordinarily moist, the desiccated coconut adds texture throughout, and the cardamom gives it the distinctive aromatic character that makes it unmistakably Kenyan. This is recipe KEN150 — the 150th and final Kenyan recipe in the GieesK Recipes collection. A fitting finale.
ingredients: 1 cup desiccated coconut — plus extra for topping
equipment: Two 20cm round cake tins or one 23cm tin
steps: Preheat oven to 180°C. Grease and line the cake tins.
Sift together flour, baking powder, bicarbonate of soda, salt, and cardamom.
Beat butter and sugar until pale and fluffy — about 5 minutes.
Add eggs one at a time, beating well after each addition.
Add vanilla and coconut extract if using.
Alternate adding the flour mixture and coconut milk in three additions, beginning and ending with flour. Fold gently.
Divide between tins. Bake for 35—40 minutes until a skewer inserted in the centre comes out clean.
Cool in tins for 10 minutes, then turn onto a wire rack to cool completely.
Whip coconut cream with icing sugar and vanilla until slightly thickened.
Fill and frost the cooled cake with coconut cream frosting. Press extra desiccated coconut onto the sides and top.
chefTips: Room temperature butter, eggs, and coconut milk are essential — cold ingredients prevent proper emulsification.
Do not overmix after adding flour — overmixing develops gluten and makes the cake tough.
The cake is done when a skewer comes out clean and the top springs back when lightly pressed.
Toast the coconut for the topping in a dry pan for extra depth.
commonMistakes: Cold butter — does not cream properly with sugar.
Overmixing after adding flour — tough, dense cake.

faqs.q: Can I make this without the frosting?
faqs.a: Yes — the cake is delicious on its own, dusted with icing sugar. The frosting adds richness but is not essential.

faqs.q: How do I store the finished cake?
faqs.a: The unfrosted cake keeps well at room temperature for 3 days. Once frosted, refrigerate and consume within 3 days. The coconut cream frosting does not keep well at room temperature in Kenyan heat.

cookingScience: Coconut milk's fat content keeps the cake crumb moist by coating the starch and protein molecules, preventing them from bonding tightly during baking. This is why coconut milk cakes stay moister longer than cakes made with water. The desiccated coconut adds fibre that also retains moisture.
sustainabilityTips: Use Kenyan coconuts and locally produced butter where possible.
Coconut palms are perennial — sustainable crop choice.
storage: Room temperature 3 days unfrosted. Refrigerate frosted cake for up to 3 days.
reheating: Not required — serve at room temperature.
healthBenefits: Best enjoyed as a celebration treat.
culturalNote: Kenyan Coconut Cake is the celebration cake of the Swahili coast and beyond — the centrepiece of every important gathering from Eid feasts in Mombasa to birthday parties in Nairobi. KEN150 is the final recipe in the 150-recipe Kenyan collection on GieesK Recipes — a fitting finale to a culinary journey through one of the world's most diverse and extraordinary food cultures.
regionalVariations: Classic coconut cake with coconut cream frosting.
